opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. The way we usually measure pre-training is pretty blunt. We track loss on a held-out set, maybe some downstream evals at checkpoints, and treat all of that as one aggregate number going down. But that number hides a lot. Most of the tokens the model sees, it has basically already learned. They're easy, they're redundant, and you're paying full compute for a tiny bit of signal.

So the first thing I'd change is to stop treating loss as one scalar and start looking at it as a distribution: per token, per domain, per type of skill. Then you can ask a much more useful question. Where is the model actually still learning, and where is it just being reminded of things it already knows? If you can measure that well, you can put compute where the marginal learning is highest. That might mean data selection, curriculum, or deciding when a batch isn't worth a full step.

The second thing is that loss and capability aren't the same. You can drive perplexity down on web text and get almost nothing on reasoning or long-horizon tasks. So I'd want cheap proxy measurements during training that correlate with the capabilities we care about, so we're not flying blind until a big eval at the end.

The third thing is the optimizer side, which is close to my heart. A lot of compute efficiency comes from how well each step uses the information in the gradient. If you measure progress in learning per FLOP rather than steps or tokens, better preconditioning and second-order-ish methods start to look much more attractive, even with some extra cost per step. The wall-clock and FLOP accounting needs to be honest, though. That includes communication, memory, and stability, not just the theoretical step count.

So in short: measure learning, not just loss. Measure it at a finer grain, tie it to capabilities, and normalize it by real compute. Once you do that, a lot of the inefficiency becomes visible, and once you can see it, you can go after it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses loss, redundancy, and marginal learning, but does not characterize pre-training as optimizing compression.

r002.rationale: It says loss and capability differ and recommends capability-correlated proxy measurements, but does not clearly argue for evaluating pre-training by end-to-end outcomes rather than perplexity.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention reinforcement learning undoing pre-training perplexity gains.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose joint pre-training and reinforcement learning or predict an order-of-magnitude compute-efficiency improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that the way we measure pre-training today is kind of a historical accident. We measure loss, we measure perplexity, and we plot it against the number of tokens or the number of FLOPs. And that's useful, it gave us scaling laws, it gave us a way to compare runs. But it also quietly bakes in an assumption, which is that every token is worth the same amount of compute, and that the only thing that matters is how much of it you push through the model.

If I were rethinking it, the first thing I'd do is stop treating tokens as the unit. The unit should be something closer to "how much did the model actually learn from this step." Because when you look inside a training run, a huge fraction of the tokens are either things the model already knows cold, so the gradient is basically noise, or things that are so far outside what it can currently represent that the gradient doesn't help either. The learning is happening in a fairly narrow band in between, and we spend compute uniformly across all of it.

So one concrete shift is measuring pre-training in terms of information gain per FLOP rather than loss per token. You can approximate that. You can look at how much the loss on a held-out slice actually moves as a function of what you fed in, and you very quickly see that the data is wildly non-uniform in value. Once you measure that way, data curation and curriculum stop being side projects and become the main lever, because now they show up directly in your efficiency metric.

The second thing is that we evaluate at the end, or at a few checkpoints, and we evaluate on benchmarks that are pretty disconnected from the training signal. I'd want much denser, much cheaper probes that track specific capabilities as they emerge during training. Not because the final benchmark doesn't matter, but because if you can see that a capability saturated at thirty percent of the run, you've just learned that the remaining seventy percent was spent on something else, and you can ask whether that something else was worth it. Right now that information is mostly invisible.

And the third piece, which I think is underrated, is measuring the optimizer and the data together rather than separately. People do sweeps on learning rate and batch size, and then separately they do ablations on data mixtures, and they treat them as independent. They're not. The right batch size depends on how redundant your data is. The right learning rate schedule depends on how the difficulty of your data evolves. If your metric is just "final loss at fixed compute," you'll never see those interactions. If your metric is something like learning efficiency over the trajectory, they jump out at you.

So to sum it up, I'd move from "how many tokens did we see" to "how much did we learn per unit of compute," I'd measure continuously instead of at the end, and I'd measure the data and the optimization process as one system. I think if you do those three things, you'd find that a lot of the compute we're spending today isn't buying us much, and that's where the efficiency is going to come from. Not from a trick, but from actually being able to see where the learning is happening.

r002.rationale: It proposes information gain per FLOP and denser capability probes; it does not argue for evaluating pre-training by end-to-end outcomes rather than perplexity.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss reinforcement learning undoing pre-training perplexity gains.

r004.rationale: The response proposes no joint pre-training and reinforcement-learning procedure or order-of-magnitude efficiency improvement.

astra-6.text:
I would start by separating two questions: how well are we predicting the next token, and how much useful capability are we getting for the compute we spend? Training loss is a very useful signal, but it’s an average over a lot of things, and not every improvement in that average translates into something we care about equally.

So I’d measure the learning curve against compute across a set of capabilities. How quickly does the model pick up a new concept? Can it apply that concept in a different context? How much repetition does it need? If you can measure those things reliably, you can start comparing changes to the data mixture, the architecture, or the optimizer in terms of how much faster they produce useful learning.

The tricky part is making sure you haven’t just built a training process that’s very good at your particular evaluations. You need held-out tasks and enough diversity to test whether the improvement generalizes. But that’s the shift I’d want: from asking only whether the loss went down to asking what the model learned, and how much compute it took to learn it.

r002.rationale: It argues for measuring useful capabilities and learning against compute, shifting beyond training loss alone to what the model learned.

r004.rationale: It does not propose joint pre-training and reinforcement learning or predict an order-of-magnitude efficiency improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start by separating two questions: how well are we predicting the next token, and how much useful capability are we getting for the compute we spend? Training loss is a useful signal, but it’s an average over a lot of very different data. An improvement there doesn’t necessarily tell you where the model is learning something valuable.

So I’d measure learning curves across a range of tasks, with compute as the budget. If we change the data mixture or the training objective, do we reach the same level of capability with fewer FLOPs? And does that improvement hold across tasks, rather than just on the benchmark we’re optimizing?

That also makes data selection part of the efficiency question. A token isn’t a fixed unit of learning. Some examples are redundant; others may teach the model something it hasn’t acquired yet. The interesting measurement is the marginal gain: given where the model is today, what should we spend the next unit of compute on?

I wouldn’t throw away next-token loss. I’d pair it with those capability measurements so we can distinguish getting better at the training distribution from learning more efficiently.
